articles.title: Gen Z needs to watch In the Mood for Love - a classic where intimacy is about grace & restraint
articles.summary: Su Li-zhen Chan (Maggie Cheug): I didn't think you'd fall in love with me. Chow Mo-wan (Tony Leung Chiu-wai): I didn't either.
articles.body: Su Li-zhen Chan (Maggie Cheug): I didn't think you'd fall in love with me. Chow Mo-wan (Tony Leung Chiu-wai): I didn't either. I was only curious to know how it started. Now I know. Feelings can creep up just like that. I thought I was in control.- In the Mood for LoveWhat if I told you the world’s best film on love is one where lovers barely touch each other? Their hands brush against one another in a couple of scenes. There are no kissing scenes or even scenes of passionate embrace. But once you watch In the Mood for Love, the 2000 masterpiece directed by Hong Kong-based Wong Kar Wai, your life will forever be changed.Love, desire, passion and relationships have all gone through a mammoth change in the 21st century. Cinema and popular culture have depicted almost all aspects of these tectonic changes; but every September 29—the day of the movie’s release in 2000—cine lovers worldwide watch In the Mood for Love yet again, and social media is abuzz as if the film had been released yesterday.Then there’s the fact that every prestigious poll on “greatest cinema” has the Wong Kar Wai classic on its top five list. Even now. The last poll was by The New York Times. In mid-2025, NYT published its milestone poll ranking the ‘100 Best Movies of the 21st Century’. Voted into the fourth position by a panel of film critics, directors and scholars was Wong Kar-wai’s masterpiece. It secured its place at the top tier of modern cinema. This high honour also builds upon decades of global critical acclaim.The film was previously placed second in the BBC’s 2016 poll of 21st-century cinema and claimed fifth place in the British Film Institute’s prestigious 2022 Sight & Sound critics' poll of the greatest films of all time. So what is it about a film where lovers just barely brush past one another that continues to draw in every generation? Even Gen X and Gen Alpha.Restraint, the invaluable currency in our hyper-connected worldWell, this film relies almost entirely on emotional restraint. To every generation first watching this film, it’s a revelation; but to this generation—so used to and exhausted with swiping right and left, and the inevitability of looking for love through an app—it hits different.We also live in an era dominated by high-budget spectacles, fast-paced editing and explicit screenwriting, and that’s what we often expect out of every love story on celluloid.In the Mood for Love does the opposite. It tells a story where the central lovers just pass one another on streets, think about each other—and their own all-encompassing loneliness—and have to keep up the pretence of being just next-door neighbours.Set in the crowded apartment blocks of 1962 Hong Kong, the narrative follows two neighbours: newspaper editor Chow Mo-wan (Tony Leung Chiu-wai) and corporate secretary Su Li-zhen (Maggie Cheung). Together, they make a painful discovery: their respective spouses are having an extramarital affair with each other.Rather than seeking sudden revenge or plunging into a physical affair of their own, Chow and Su draw close through shared grief. They role-play imaginary conversations to figure out how their partners betrayed them, while silently making a solemn promise to themselves: “We won’t be like them”. But they do fall in love with one another. And that promise hangs in the balance.The late legendary movie critic Roger Ebert had wrote about the film: "They are in the mood for love, but not in the time and place for it. They look at each other with big damp eyes of yearning and sweetness, and go home to sleep by themselves. Adultery has sullied their lives: his wife and her husband are having an affair. “For us to do the same thing,” they agree, “would mean we are no better than they are.” The key word there is “agree.” The fact is, they do not agree. It is simply that neither one has the courage to disagree, and time is passing..."Through this vow of self-control, Wong Kar-wai delivers a powerful and unforgettable emotional experience. His love is not an act of physical possession at all. It is a lingering, unfulfilled state of longing that stays in memory forever. It cuts you to pieces. Every scene. From the beginning till the end.For 21st-century audiences living in a hyper-connected world, this movie can feel like a meditation. Nothing in this movie is explicitly said or made obvious. Wong's vision of intimacy is this: true closeness is often born from what remains unsaid, untouched and unconsumed.The power of what is unsaid but lingers in the airTo understand Wong Kar-wai’s artistic genius, we must examine his definition of intimacy. In traditional romance movies, intimacy is usually shown through physical touch, explicit confessions or sexual union. Wong completely flips this formula.In his cinematic universe, physical contact is often brief or misleading, whereas true intimacy flourishes in shared spaces, quiet silences and mutual understanding.Reflecting on his storytelling approach, Wong explained the main direction he gave to actress Maggie Cheung during filming: “We’re not making a movie about what’s said – we’re making one about what’s hidden”.This idea forms the core of his aesthetic. Intimacy in In the Mood for Love is built through delicate body language, small gestures and the physical environment. Wong instructed his lead actors to let their hands do the talking, noting that hands betray what faces hide, and that desire lives in subtle details like holding a cigarette, holding a letter or touching the edge of a dress.This focus on small gestures is tied to the physical setting of 1960s Hong Kong. He recalled how tiny living spaces forced people together with no privacy. Life was an open book read over one’s shoulder, creating thick human connections inside buildings with paper-thin walls.In such a tight environment, romance could not be displayed openly without causing neighbourhood gossip and social shame. As a result, intimacy shifted into quiet daily routines, like, brushing past one another on narrow stairwells while carrying takeaway noodle tins, standing under rain-soaked awnings or waiting in dim hallways.Did the rice cooker change the definition of love?Wong pointed out that simple daily inventions like rice cookers, instant noodles and 24-hour convenience stores changed Asian intimacy far more deeply than romantic love letters, because these objects altered how people moved through space and met each other every day.For instance, when Chow and Su practise role-playing scenarios to understand their spouses' affair, they create a private emotional world. They pretend to confront each other, flirt and say goodbye. Yet, as they act out these scenes, the line between performance and reality begins to disappear. They fall in love by sharing the exact weight of their heartbreak. For instance, in a restaurant while having dinner, and both heartbroken by their spouses' betrayal, Chow orders Su's husband's favourite dish, and Su asks for Chow's wife's favourite. While biting into each piece both the protagonists are trying to process grief and trying to understand each other's spouses, who are having the affair. The scene is at once - jarring, uncomfortable, intimate and absolute heartbreak.Then of course, is Wong Kar-wai's brilliant choice of cinematography and music, which are main characters in this movie - as essential as the protagonists. Christopher Doyle, the cinematographer, and Yumeji's Theme, the main soundtrack of the film, composed by Shigeru Umebayashi.While In the Mood for Love takes place in 1962 and was released in 2000, its core themes continue to resonate with audiences today. Modern life is filled with rapid digital communication, dating apps, instant text messages and social media oversharing. Relationships can start quickly and end just as fast, with romance often reduced to quick interactions and immediate responses.Against this backdrop, the film’s slow unfolding feels striking. There is time to notice a glance, a pause, a hesitation. Feelings are allowed to exist without immediately being named or acted upon. The characters’ silences become as important as their conversations, and what they choose not to do becomes the most important part of the story.The film also leaves us with an intriguing idea about unfulfilled desire. What remains unresolved can acquire a strange permanence because it never has the opportunity to become ordinary. Chow and Su’s relationship remains suspended between possibility and impossibility – protected from the routines and compromises that might have accompanied another life together. That is why it continues to feel so intimate.The everlasting echo of unfulfilled desireThis turn-of-the-millennium movie is a major achievement in global cinema also because it captures a feeling that can transcend culture and age: the ache of wanting something that can never quite become yours.Its fourth-place spot on The New York Times list of the top 100 movies of the 21st century is only the latest recognition of a film that has remained remarkably alive in popular and critical culture.Through its rich colours, small physical gestures and expressive music, the film shows how much emotional weight can be carried by the smallest moments.That is the secret of its enduring appeal. In the Mood for Love does not give us the satisfaction of a conventional love story with a beginning, middle and resolution. It leaves us with a feeling — unfinished, unresolved and lingering. The romance ends, but the longing remains, suspended somewhere between memory and imagination.Maybe that’s why, more than two decades after its release, we keep returning to it.You use AI every day. articles.title: In 2025, about a dozen Getty Villa workers stayed as the Palisades Fire reached the grounds, fighting spot fires and sealing galleries; the museum and ancient art survived untouched
articles.summary: In January 2025, Getty Villa employees bravely fought to save the museum's priceless Greek and Roman art from the devastating Palisades Fire, demonstrating the importance of preparation and emergency response in the face of natural disasters.
articles.body: Museums are designed to last for centuries, but a single windy afternoon can still endanger a collection. Ancient ceramics, bronze and marble have survived graves, wars and earthquakes, and once they are lost, they cannot be restored. That was the risk facing the Getty Villa, a Pacific Palisades museum of Greek and Roman art, when a brush fire was reported about two miles away on January 7, 2025.It turned out that a combination of astute engineering and courageous individuals was the solution. According to Getty, every employee except about a dozen security and facilities volunteers went home. Those who stayed worked from the Villa's Emergency Operations Center, sealed the museum doors and put out small fires around the grounds while the main fire burnt nearby.When the smoke cleared, the buildings of the Villa were unharmed, and the art inside was undamaged, although the grounds did lose a considerable number of trees. This is not a call for ordinary people to stay put when told to evacuate. The Villa appears to have benefited from a detailed emergency plan, a purpose-built site and a direct line to fire authorities. Their experience offers lessons on preparation.A museum built for fireThe Villa had been built with fire in mind long before that January day. Getty says its walls are reinforced concrete beneath a tiled roof, and fire-rated doors can prevent smoke or flames from spreading to the rest of the site. A carbon-filtered air conditioner maintains a steady flow of pressure, which can be increased to keep out smoke and ash. In each room, detectors are set to an extremely low threshold to detect a fire at its earliest stage.The sprinklers are a surprise. They are kept absolutely dry to avoid accidental water damage and are only used as a last option. In case of loss of the main utility pressure, a backup water reservoir will serve the site. Emergency generators will operate the fire systems and lighting for weeks.Outside, the gardens had been constructed with fire in mind. The property is surrounded by oak trees, which absorb water effectively and burn more slowly than other plants; an irrigation system keeps the soil moist; and grounds staff clear low brush throughout the year, working beyond the distance the Los Angeles Fire Department requires.Timing also helped: the Villa was closed to the public on Tuesdays, so no visitors were on site when the fire arrived. Getty’s emergency preparedness specialist, Les Borsay, was testing the fire alarm system around 10 a.m. on Jan. 7 when a phone warning came in reporting a brush fire about two miles away. Within two hours, he said, it was already quite near. But buildings don’t put out a fire on a lawn, and that’s where the crew came in.Inside the long dayThe scale of the fire explains why the Villa could not count on outside help. CAL FIRE said the Palisades Fire began at 10:30 a.m. on Jan. 7, 2025, burned 23,448 acres before it was fully contained on Jan. 31, destroyed 6,845 structures, damaged 975 others and killed 12 civilians. As the fire spread, thousands of structures were in its path, and crews could not be committed to any one siteWithin the Villa the volunteers got themselves organised. The engineering manager monitored the humidity levels in the galleries and took action when alarms sounded, switching building systems to safeguard the collection and sealing the museum doors. The teams at the Villa and at the Getty Center in Brentwood checked security cameras for signs of flames, and the Center's personnel assisted in sending warnings when some radios at the Villa stopped working. Others patrolled in security vehicles, keeping watch on weak spots such as a parking area where cars would have been dangerous if they caught fire.Staff took turns during the day and into the night to step into the hot, smoky air and put out tiny flames with extinguishers, shovels or their boots. They put on N95 masks and goggles and were warned to return indoors after 20 to 30 minutes. Fires broke out in rosemary vines near the visitor car park, in plants above the Outdoor Classical Theatre, and immediately outside the front gate.“The difficulty was the wind; as soon as one fire was extinguished, another popped up behind them,” said security supervisor Carl Gordon. “My crew used at least 40 five-pound extinguishers.” None of them were firefighters. “I was at the Villa for 28 hours straight,” adds Borsay. Others stayed for 72 hours, sleeping in turns. Flames were near. The team dialled 911 to direct firemen to adjacent fires. Water was dropped by air on a slope near to the Ranch House, the first Getty museum, and firefighters were welcome to fill their vehicles from the Villa’s 50,000-gallon water tank.What other museums can learnUS Forest Service scientist Jack Cohen's research suggests that whether a home ignites during an extreme wildfire is largely determined by the house and its surroundings within about 100 feet, with flying embers and small surface fires among the main threats. That is consistent with the villa's practice of cutting brush early and keeping the soil damp. It also suggests why putting out small fires promptly can make a difference.The Getty team has been candid about what did not go so well. "The modest five- and 10-pound extinguishers we used were never intended for brush fires," Borsay told ABC7. Getty staff have since told other cultural institutions that water-based extinguishers work better than dry chemical ones in strong wind, and that staff should be sent home early.There was also the human side. Gordon said family members continued asking him why he had not left. After 30 years at the Villa, he said he felt a sense of responsibility for the institution. Security staff also handed out food, drink and torches to stranded neighbours nearby.About a dozen volunteers stayed at the Villa, but they did so under a plan, with training and with fire services close at hand. For everyone else, the official advice remains the same: when evacuation orders are issued, leave. Let preparation done ahead of time do the work.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: In 2025, two brothers stayed through California’s Eaton Fire to protect their parents’ 65-year-old home; they saved it and, their family says, helped save nearby homes too
articles.summary: In a heroic act during California's Eaton Fire, brothers Justin and his sibling defended their family's 65-year-old home, saving it and potentially nearby houses from destruction. Follow their courageous journey as they battle the flames to protect their mother's legacy.
articles.body: Justin Murphy had gotten his 93-year-old mother, Jane, out of their Altadena home when the Eaton Fire began bearing down on the neighborhood in the early hours of Jan. 8, 2025, following which he went back to the house with his brother. The two spent the night using hoses and sprinklers to fight the fire and protect the property, which their parents had bought 65 years earlier. The main home survived, although a detached garage and study were destroyed, KQED reported in March 2025.The Murphy home stood on a secluded cul-de-sac in northeast Altadena with views toward the San Gabriel Mountains, and KQED reported that eight homes had stood on the street for more than a century. It was declared contained on Jan. 31 after 24 days. The immediate problem for the Murphys was to keep the flames from taking hold of the property. Justin later told KQED that he believed that their actions prevented the fire from gaining a foothold in the house. He created a text chain that provided updates to more than a dozen people who had left the area. There were checkpoints that restricted access to Altadena after the fire, and those updates became one way for residents outside the neighborhood to learn what was happening around their homes.Los Angeles County's recovery records now describe the Eaton Fire as a massive wildfire that consumed more than 14,000 acres and destroyed more than 9,000 structures in Altadena. The county continues to operate recovery programs for residents whose homes and properties were damaged or destroyed.The fire moved through Altadena under extreme conditionsThe Eaton Fire started at about 6:18 p.m. on Jan. 7, according to the final CAL FIRE record, and the agency lists the cause as electrical. On Jan. 8, the record described strong winds, low humidity and dry fuels that were contributing to rapid fire growth and spot fires. The Murphy house was among the small number of properties that remained standing on its street. The garage and study were gone, but the main residence was still usable.Returning to a neighborhood that had changedJustin remained in Altadena after the immediate danger passed while much of the neighborhood was still under restrictions. KQED reported that military-enforced security checkpoints prevented many people from returning for roughly two weeks. Murphy was detained several times while moving around the area, but if he left through a checkpoint, it could mean losing the ability to return.His mother eventually went back to the house once the checkpoints were lifted, and KQED reported that she resumed her regular two-mile walks through the neighborhood even as burned properties surrounded her. The family's house was still standing, but the street around it had been transformed; it had once been eight homes but was reduced to two. articles.title: A Michigan woman entrusted with managing Social Security benefits for her elderly disabled uncle allegedly took nearly $121,000 over seven years while prosecutors say he lived without running water, electricity or heat
articles.summary: A case from Michigan is among several Social Security fraud cases announced by the US Department of Justice as part of a nationwide enforcement effort
articles.body: A case from Michigan is among several Social Security fraud cases announced by the US Department of Justice as part of a nationwide enforcement effort targeting the misuse of federal benefits. According to the US Department of Justice (DOJ), Laura Whisenant allegedly misused nearly $121,000 in Social Security benefits belonging to her elderly, mentally disabled uncle over a period of seven years. The DOJ says Whisenant was serving as his representative payee, a role that allowed her to manage the benefits on his behalf. Prosecutors allege that while the money was being misused, her uncle was living in extremely poor conditions, in a house without running water, electricity or heat. The allegations form part of a broader September 2026 DOJ announcement detailing criminal cases involving more than $1.3 million in intended losses to the US government. Whisenant has been charged under federal law concerning the misuse of Social Security benefits. Because the case is based on a complaint, the allegations against her have not been proven in court.She was responsible for managing her uncle’s benefitsWhisenant's role in the case is significant because she was not simply accused of accessing someone else's Social Security payments. According to the DOJ, she had been appointed as the representative payee for her elderly, mentally disabled uncle. A representative payee is responsible for receiving and managing Social Security benefits for someone who is unable to manage those benefits independently. The money is meant to be used for the beneficiary's needs.According to the DOJ complaint, Whisenant allegedly used that position to take and misuse nearly $121,000 in her uncle's Social Security benefits over seven years. The department lists the intended loss associated with the case as $121,980. The allegation covers a considerable period, meaning the purported misuse was not described as a single withdrawal or isolated incident. Prosecutors say the benefits were misused over seven years while Whisenant was serving in the representative-payee role.Prosecutors say her uncle was living without basic utilitiesThe circumstances surrounding the alleged misuse are a central part of the case. According to the DOJ, Whisenant's uncle was living in a house without running water, electricity or heat while she allegedly misused his benefits. The department described him as elderly and mentally disabled. That detail is particularly important because representative payees are entrusted with managing benefits for people who may need assistance handling their own finances. The money is intended to support the beneficiary rather than serve as a source of personal funds for the person managing it.The case was part of a wider Social Security fraud crackdownWhisenant's case was announced alongside several other federal cases involving alleged theft or misuse of Social Security benefits. The Justice Department said its National Fraud Enforcement Division, working with US Attorneys' Offices in 11 districts and the Social Security Administration's Office of Inspector General, brought charges against 17 defendants between August 21 and September 18. The department said those defendants were allegedly responsible for more than $1.3 million in intended losses to the United States. The cases involved different types of alleged conduct.In one case from Illinois, prosecutors accused a woman of concealing her deceased mother's body in a freezer while allegedly continuing to collect her mother's Social Security and other benefits. Another defendant in New York was accused of continuing to withdraw money from his deceased brother's account after his death while Social Security payments continued to be deposited. Other cases involved people who allegedly acted as representative payees for relatives or children receiving benefits. The DOJ said the cases were part of a broader effort to identify and prosecute fraud involving Social Security Administration benefit programmes, including Supplemental Security Income.What happens next in the Michigan caseThe federal charge against Whisenant concerns 42 U.S.C. § 408(a)(5), a provision relating to fraud, misrepresentation or misuse involving Social Security benefits. The DOJ lists a maximum penalty of five years in prison for the charge. That maximum penalty does not mean that a particular sentence will be imposed. The outcome of a criminal case depends on the court proceedings, evidence, applicable sentencing rules and other factors. For now, the allegations remain allegations. The DOJ's announcement identifies the case as a complaint, rather than announcing a conviction or sentence. The case also highlights the responsibility that comes with managing government benefits for someone who cannot manage them independently. In this instance, prosecutors allege that nearly $121,000 in benefits were misused over seven years while the elderly beneficiary lived without basic household utilities.The broader DOJ enforcement action shows that representative-payee arrangements are one of several areas being examined as federal authorities pursue alleged Social Security fraud. For Whisenant, the next stage will be the federal court process, where the allegations outlined by prosecutors can be tested against the evidence and a final legal determination can be made.You use AI every day. articles.title: Pilot stabbed, chaos in cockpit & sudden plunge: How disaster was averted on flydubai flight, explained in 10 points
articles.summary: A routine flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv turned into a terrifying mid-air emergency on Wednesday after an apparent violent confrontation between the pilots
articles.body: A routine flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv turned into a terrifying mid-air emergency on Wednesday after an apparent violent confrontation between the pilots of a flydubai aircraft. Flight FZ1073, carrying around 180 people, was forced to divert to Saudi Arabia after transmitting emergency signals, including the international code associated with unlawful interference.The Boeing 737 was flying towards Israel when its altitude suddenly dropped sharply. Flight-tracking data showed the aircraft descending by thousands of feet in a matter of seconds, while passengers reported hearing screams coming from the cockpit. The situation became even more alarming when the aircraft transmitted the 7500 transponder code, which is used to indicate hijacking or unlawful interference.Also read: Passengers recall harrowing ordeal on flight that nearly crashedHere is what happened:A routine Dubai-Tel Aviv flight suddenly went wrongFlydubai flight FZ1073 took off from Dubai International Airport bound for Ben Gurion Airport near Tel Aviv. The route is a regular one, with flydubai operating daily return services between the UAE and Israel.The aircraft was a Boeing 737 Max 8 and had around 180 people on board, according to reports. The first part of the journey appeared to be routine. But roughly two and a half hours after departure, the aircraft suddenly began losing altitude.Also read: Screams, chaos onboard as Flydubai flight takes 17,000 ft roller coaster ride mid-airFlight-tracking data showed a dramatic descent from cruising altitude, with different reports putting the fall at around 14,000 to 17,400 feet in a short period. The aircraft then changed course towards Saudi Arabia instead of continuing towards Israel.What caused the sudden descent was initially unclear. Soon, however, reports emerged that something had gone seriously wrong inside the cockpit.Screams, blood and a fight inside the cockpitPassengers later described a chaotic scene. One passenger, identified as Miriam, told Israeli media that passengers heard screaming before the cockpit door opened.She said they saw a large amount of blood and that one of the pilots appeared to have been injured. Another account said a man carrying a knife had forced one of the pilots to the floor.Also read: Pilot tried to crash plane, hijack code triggered - What happened on Tel Aviv flightAn Israeli official told Reuters that the pilots had been involved in a physical altercation. Later reports from Israeli officials went further, saying information gathered during the investigation indicated that the co-pilot may have tried to stab the captain.The precise sequence remains under investigation. Passenger accounts provide a picture of panic inside the aircraft, but they do not by themselves establish exactly what happened in the cockpit or why the confrontation began.The plane suddenly plunged thousands of feetThe most alarming indication of what was happening came from the aircraft's flight path. Tracking data showed that FZ1073 underwent a sudden and steep descent while flying over the region.One set of data showed the aircraft falling nearly 14,000 feet in less than 30 seconds, while other reports put the total descent at more than 17,000 feet in roughly two minutes.Passengers reportedly felt the aircraft dip sharply and feared that they were going to die. One passenger described the plane as being "completely out of control".The descent occurred around the same time as the reported confrontation between the pilots. However, flight-tracking data can establish what the aircraft did, not necessarily why it happened. Investigators will have to establish whether the descent resulted directly from the cockpit struggle or from deliberate action by one of the pilots.Why the hijack scareThe aircraft initially transmitted the 7700 transponder code, which signals a general emergency. Several minutes later, it transmitted 7500, the internationally recognised code for unlawful interference and commonly associated with hijacking.That immediately transformed the incident into a major security alert.The aircraft was travelling towards Israel, carrying a large number of Israeli passengers, and the 7500 signal raised fears that someone could have attempted to seize control of the plane.Israel responded by scrambling fighter jets as authorities tried to determine what was happening. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu also held security consultations as the incident unfolded.The 7500 signal was therefore critical in triggering the response, although it remained unclear who transmitted the code and under what circumstances.Israel feared the worst, but it was not a conventional hijackingThe initial response was based on the possibility that the aircraft had been hijacked. But Israeli officials later said the incident did not appear to be a conventional hijacking.Doron Spielman, a spokesperson for the Israeli prime minister's office, told Reuters that the incident was not believed to have been a hijacking and described it as a "different incident".That distinction became important as more information emerged about the alleged cockpit fight.According to Israeli officials cited in later reports, the confrontation may have involved one pilot attempting to overpower the other. Some officials said they were examining the possibility that the incident was an attempted attack, while the investigation remained ongoing.Passengers and other crew members reportedly intervenedOne of the most extraordinary elements of the incident was the reported intervention of people inside the aircraft.According to Israeli reports, passengers helped restrain the pilot who was allegedly attacking the other pilot. This account has not been independently established in every detail, but officials said passengers and crew members became involved after the confrontation escalated.Reports also said there was another group of pilots travelling as passengers on the aircraft, dressed in civilian clothes. According to a Channel 12 report cited by The Times of Israel, these pilots helped prevent one of the pilots from taking over the aircraft.If confirmed, their presence would have provided an additional layer of assistance during an extraordinary emergency in which the operating flight crew had become incapacitated or involved in a physical struggle.A second team of pilots may have helped avert disasterThe report that other pilots were travelling as passengers is particularly significant. According to Israeli media, these pilots were able to help after the cockpit confrontation and prevent the situation from becoming even more serious.A senior Israeli official was quoted as saying that without the additional pilots, the incident could potentially have resulted in a catastrophic outcome. The official compared the potential consequences to major past attacks, although that assessment remains an official characterisation rather than an established outcome.The precise role played by the off-duty pilots has not been fully detailed publicly. However, reports indicate that they helped ensure the aircraft could remain under control after the fight between the operating pilots.Why did the aircraft land in Saudi Arabia?Once the aircraft was stabilised, it was diverted towards Saudi Arabia rather than continuing to Israel.Flight-tracking data showed the aircraft changing course and eventually heading towards Tabuk in northwestern Saudi Arabia. It landed safely at Tabuk airport, where Saudi security forces surrounded the aircraft.The decision was logical in the circumstances because the aircraft required an immediate emergency landing after the cockpit incident. Tabuk provided a suitable airport for the aircraft to land while authorities dealt with the situation.Both pilots were later reported to have been taken to hospital after suffering injuries. The airline said all passengers were safe and accounted for and that its teams were working with the relevant authorities.How close was this to becoming a mass-casualty disaster?The full answer will depend on the investigation. Israeli officials have described the incident as one in which a major disaster was narrowly avoided, while some officials are examining whether the incident amounted to an attempted attack.But several elements are already clear. The aircraft suffered a dramatic loss of altitude, a fight reportedly broke out between the pilots, at least one pilot was injured, an emergency code associated with unlawful interference was transmitted and fighter jets were scrambled.Passengers also described seeing blood and hearing screams, while the aircraft had to divert to another country.What remains unclear is the motive, exactly who initiated the violence, who transmitted the emergency codes and whether the descent was deliberate. Those questions will determine how the incident is ultimately classified.A horrific reminderThe incident has inevitably brought back memories of the Germanwings disaster, one of the most devastating cases involving deliberate action by a pilot. On March 24, 2015, Germanwings Flight 9525, an Airbus A320 flying from Barcelona to Düsseldorf, crashed in the French Alps, killing all 150 people on board.Investigators concluded that the co-pilot deliberately locked the captain out of the cockpit and initiated the aircraft's descent, preventing the captain from regaining control.The Germanwings crash subsequently led to renewed debate over cockpit access, pilot monitoring and aviation safety procedures.The circumstances surrounding the flydubai incident are different and remain under investigation. The aircraft landed safely and all passengers survived. But the reported combination of a cockpit confrontation, a steep descent, emergency signals and alleged attempts to seize control highlights the potentially catastrophic consequences when the people responsible for flying an aircraft become part of an in-flight security emergency.You use AI every day. And one woman with three children went to the (cockpit) and saw a lot of blood," Abukasis told AFP while waiting at Ben Gurion Airport near Tel Aviv.She said her daughter had called her after landing and told her that everyone "thought they were going to die".The incident reportedly triggered a security alert after the aircraft transmitted emergency signals, prompting Israel to scramble fighter jets amid fears of a possible hijacking. It added that the Reef Program completed the deployment with the help of the New Jersey Department of Environmental Protection and its Aids to Navigation.Who donated the gravestones to New Jersey’s artificial reef programThe material was donated to the NJ Artificial Reef Program. articles.summary: Trump lost 41 House seats in his first term's midterms, but Ronald Reagan's playbook of heralding American heroes offers Republicans a path forward.
articles.body: Now in the autumn of this critical political season, a midterm loss of Congress for Republicans feels inevitable, as the last five midterm elections saw the party in power lose seats in Congress. This trend goes back even longer than the 2000s. Since 1946, the president’s party has lost seats in the U.S. House of Representatives in 18 of 20 midterm elections (90% of the time). President Donald Trump ran into this trend in his first term when, in 2018, Republicans lost 41 seats in the House — though they did gain two seats in the U.S. Senate. MIDTERM HISTORY MASSIVELY FAVORS DEMOCRATS. BUT THEY ARE MAKING A BIG MISTAKE Despite the pattern, a loss is not inevitable. Consider Ronald Reagan’s 1980 election eve address "A Vision for America." This speech came at a time of great national peril and discontentment, so, to give clarity to his positive vision, Reagan drew on American heroes from astronauts to John Wayne: "Last year I lost a friend who was more than a symbol of the Hollywood dream industry; to millions he was a symbol of our country itself. And when he died, the headlines seemed to convey all the doubt about America, all the nostalgia for a seemingly lost past. REPUBLICANS NEED A REAGAN-STYLE VISION TO WIN THE BATTLE OVER AMERICA'S FUTURE "'The Last American Hero,' said one headline, ‘Mr. America dies,’ said another. "Well, I knew John Wayne well, and no one would have been angrier at being called the 'last American hero.' "Just before his death, he said in his own blunt way, 'Just give the American people a good cause, and there’s nothing they can’t lick.'" Republicans have done a poor job giving the American people a good cause. The thing is, the right cause is what led to the two exceptions. REPUBLICANS FACE BRUTAL MIDTERM HEADWINDS. SIX FORCES COULD HELP THEM DEFY HISTORY. The last exception to the party in power losing seats in a midterm was in 2002, when Republicans under George W. Bush gained eight seats. This occurred during a time of high presidential approval ratings after the 9/11 terrorist attacks. The other modern exception was in 1998, when Democrats gained five seats under Bill Clinton during a time of high presidential approval thanks to a strong economy (ironically, in part because Republicans, under Speaker Newt Gingrich, balanced the budget and strong-armed a temporarily weakened Clinton into agreeing to welfare reform). So, both of these exceptions came at times of strong national unity. But, to be more precise, the exceptions came when voters rallied to the party in power for largely nationalistic reasons. This, if articulated cleanly, could and should benefit Republicans, as the Democrats have turned so far left that the Democratic Socialists of America’s (DSA) official platform now feels like it could be the next platform for the party of Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., and Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed. OUR CLOSING ARGUMENT: THE MIDTERMS ARE A REFERENDUM ON WHO RUNS YOUR LIFE But how can Republicans not only show this stark contrast to voters, but also unleash a national fervor for truth, justice, and the American way, as the American comic book hero Superman once put it? As Reagan did, the best way to do this is to herald our heroes. America has innovators, entrepreneurs, capitalists, and heroes in blue and green; we have armed citizens who defend themselves and others; we have civil-rights champions like Harmeet Dhillon; we have explorers who would go back to the moon and then to Mars thanks to entrepreneurs like Elon Musk... these and other heroes can also be juxtaposed beside the so-called heroes of today’s left (the deep-state bureaucrats, anti-Israel activists, open-border politicians, proponents of allowing men into women’s sports, gun grabbers, and more) to show who is actually for American freedom. Do voters want the low taxes, pro-freedom agenda of, say, Florida’s Gov. Ron DeSantis, or do they want the high taxes and increasing special-interest squalor of Gov. Gavin Newsom’s California? Do voters want our heroes in blue to maintain what is now the lowest violent-crime rate America has seen in more than half a century, or do they want George Soros-backed district attorneys to give criminals get-out-of-jail-free cards again and again so they can prey on us? Do voters want Secretary of Health and Human Services Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s Make America Healthy Again (MAHA) movement to let us know what is in our food and more, or do they want big food to go back to writing our guidelines? Do voters want to be led by an elite class of "experts," such as we were during Covid by Anthony Fauci, or do they want the individual autonomy to freely decide for themselves? Each issue needs to be shown in vivid and very human terms. Reagan, again, understood this. Near the end of his "Vision for America" speech, Reagan spoke of American astronauts who had lost their lives in the quest to reach the moon before saying, "These were not the deeds of men who set out to be heroes. In many ways, they were ordinary Americans whose spontaneous response to time and circumstance gave us a glimpse into the soul of this country and the enduring vigor of her people." articles.title: Grooming gangs inquiry expanded to Birmingham and Wales
articles.summary: Targeted investigations will be carried out as part of a national inquiry into child sexual abuse.
articles.body:
A national inquiry into child sexual abuse by grooming gangs has announced that targeted investigations will take place in Birmingham and Wales.

The inquiry said the probes would "examine the sexual abuse and exploitation of children by grooming gangs and the response of organisations responsible for protecting children" in both areas.

Oldham in Greater Manchester, Bradford and Keighley in West Yorkshire and London were announced as the first locations for investigations earlier this year.

It is unclear whether further locations will be selected. Some survivors have expressed frustration that their area has not yet been included and said they were concerned about expanding the inquiry's scope.

Fiona Goddard, who was sexually abused as a child by groups of men in Bradford, said there was clearly evidence from Birmingham and Wales "that needs to be properly heard" and welcomed their inclusion.

But she told the BBC that the scale of the inquiry "must not come at the expense of the depth of investigation". This was especially concerning, Goddard added, given "we are already almost a year into the inquiry with relatively little progress".

Carly, not her real name, was 12 years old when she was first groomed in Huddersfield in 2004. She said she could not understand "how an investigation covering an area as enormous and complex as Wales can be described as a deep dive".

"How are survivors in Huddersfield supposed to have confidence that our experiences will not simply be absorbed into a much bigger national picture and effectively watered down?"

Meanwhile, Welsh grooming gang victim Emily Vaughan, not her real name, welcomed the announcement - saying it marked "a day that has been needed for a very long time".

"It's about institutions that failed children and the questions that have remained unanswered. The expansion of the inquiry means those failures can no longer simply be brushed aside."

The Statutory Independent Inquiry into Grooming Gangs in England and Wales was announced by former Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer in June 2025 and started work in April.

It previously faced turbulence prior to launching, when abuse survivors called on former safeguarding minister Jess Phillips to quit amid claims that the government was seeking to widen the scope of the inquiry to other forms of child abuse.

Chaired by former children's commissioner Baroness Anne Longfield, it has the power to compel individuals and institutions to explain what they "did or did not do to protect children from being sexually abused".

Alongside national accountability hearings, local investigations will examine what happened in specific areas, including how grooming gangs operated and what institutions knew.

The inquiry has previously said that areas are chosen for investigation based on criteria including how victims and survivors were treated when they came forward, and whether opportunities to prevent harm were missed.

A National Listening Project, inviting victims and survivors to share their experiences, has also been expanded, with people able to contribute through written or recorded submissions from next month.

But Amy Clowrey, a director at Switalskis solicitors, which represents more than 50 survivors who are participating in the national inquiry, warned that clarity was needed over how evidence "from places without a local investigation" would be examined by the inquiry.

First locations for grooming gang inquiry announced

Hundreds of my abusers are still out there, says victim as grooming inquiry launched

Vital paperwork for grooming gangs inquiry may be lost, say MPs

The inquiry said its decision to conduct an investigation in Birmingham reflected a combination of factors "including victim and survivor experience, indications of prevalence, harm and risk, and public concern".

Panel member Zoë Billingham said: "We will look carefully at what organisations knew, how decisions were made, how agencies worked together, and why opportunities to protect children were missed".

The Birmingham investigation may extend to surrounding or connected areas if the evidence supports it.

Phillips, Labour MP for Birmingham Yardley, welcomed the move. She praised Baroness Longfield as an "amazing and robust" public servant, adding that those already taking part in the inquiry "felt that they've been heard".

But she said her main hope for the inquiry was for it to create "the impetus for change", adding that she did not want the process "to go on for decades".

Birmingham Local Conservatives, which had previously called for the city's grooming cases to be fully investigated, also welcomed the announcement - saying questions had gone unanswered for too long.

The investigation in Wales will also examine the operation of devolved arrangements and cross-border working between organisations in Wales and England.

The Welsh government welcomed the announcement, and said minister Delyth Jewell had met Baroness Longfield earlier this week to press for "dedicated activity" in Wales as part of the national inquiry.

The Welsh Conservatives and Reform also supported the news. Both parties have previously called for a Wales-only grooming gangs inquiry, but failed to win support from the government under both Welsh Labour and Plaid Cymru.

Additional reporting by David Deans and Trystan Jones.

articles.title: Iran urges Americans to rally against Trump ahead of midterms
articles.summary: Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) on Tuesday called on Americans to vote against President Trump ahead of the midterm elections to change U.S. policy toward Tehran and accept the offer of a “peaceful coexistence.” IRGC spokesperson Gen. Hossein Mohebbi made the request in a 25-page letter, marking seven months since Iran’s conflict with the…
articles.body:
Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) on Tuesday called on Americans to vote against President Trump ahead of the midterm elections to change U.S. policy toward Tehran and accept the offer of a “peaceful coexistence.”

IRGC spokesperson Gen. Hossein Mohebbi made the request in a 25-page letter , marking seven months since Iran’s conflict with the U.S. and Israel began in late February.

“You are the ones who empower, with your votes, the government and allow it to do what it does,” the letter, obtained by The Times of Israel , reads. “Although American politicians often win your votes through deception and false promises, as Trump did, you can change the makeup of the government if you apply the criteria for good leadership in choosing the people you vote into office.”

The IRGC also suggested the U.S. and Israel are losing the war, while noting the United States is a great nation. But, he added, “to allow vulgar and immoral individuals to continue steering your politics and policies will only further humiliate and undermine the U.S.”

“Any politician who thinks they can buy your vote for $5,000 is unworthy to lead you,” the letter continues. “Take back control.”

Mohebbi later told The Associated Press that Americans should take to the streets to rally against the Trump administration and denounce what he called its warmongering policies. He accused the U.S. of attempting to turn Iran “back into a colony” in focusing on its nuclear program, which Iranian officials have long said is for peaceful purposes.

White House communications director Steven Cheung blasted the IRGC’s letter.

“This garbage ‘letter’ is a farcical and laughable attempt by a desperate group of people (IRGC) who know they have no other options left because they have failed their own people, so they resort to telling the American people to ‘vote Democrat,'” Cheung wrote on the social platform X .

“People are smarter than that and they know supporting extreme liberal Democrats means supporting groups like the IRGC,” Cheung added.

The regime indicated Wednesday that they received an official response from the U.S. to Tehran’s seven-day peace proposal , which was rejected by Trump on Saturday. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi presented the latest response to President Masoud Pezeshkian during a Cabinet meeting, government spokesperson Fatemeh Mohajerani posted to the social platform X .

“We will make every effort to bring the agreement to fruition and will firmly stand up for the rights of the Iranian people,” Pezeshkian said, according to the AP . “The agreement must now be based on a win-win strategy.”

The Iran war has been a key issue going into the midterms, with Democratic candidates slamming the administration for dragging the U.S. into another conflict in the Middle East and Republicans calling for its swift end to lower soaring gas prices caused by Iran’s closure of the Strait of Hormuz.

Trump and other administration officials said the conflict would last days or weeks in the months after the first strikes on Feb. 28. Mounting concern among voters over high gas prices and the conflict’s unpopularity has largely been dismissed, as the president said in April that he did not consider Americans’ financial hardships when determining the path forward on Iran.

He told voters at a rally in North Carolina for Republican Senate hopeful Michael Whatley earlier this month that rising gas prices were “a very inexpensive price to pay” in the U.S.’s confrontation with Iran.

“But that’s going to come tumbling down,” he added, referring to the energy costs. “That’s going to be like rocket ships in reverse.”

The national average price for gas dipped slightly on Wednesday, reaching $4.43 after previously being closer to $4.50 earlier this week, according to AAA .

articles.title: Trump’s handling of Venezuela’s oil money threatens a constitutional crisis
articles.summary: The problem here isn’t Venezuela. It is Trump.
articles.body:
Buried inside President Trump’s takeover of Venezuela’s oil revenue is a ticking constitutional time-bomb.

For months, congressional Democrats have been asking questions about Trump’s financial system for controlling Venezuelan assets. But despite repeated hearings, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent will not give Congress a basic accounting of the billions in Venezuelan oil money and other assets that the Trump administration has been collecting and managing through a series of elusive bank accounts. Nor is there clear constitutional or congressional authority for any of this.

The arrangement began after Trump ordered the U.S. military to capture former Venezuelan president Nicolas Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, from their bedchamber, bringing them to the U.S. to await trial on alleged criminal violations. Maduro’s vice president, Delcy Rodriguez, was installed as interim Venezuelan president and later recognized by the U.S. government.

After announcing in January that Venezuela would turn over up to 50 million barrels of oil to the U.S., Trump stated that the oil “will be controlled by me … to ensure it is used to benefit the people of Venezuela and the United States!”

The White House formalized the arrangement on January in an executive order stating that the funds remain Venezuelan sovereign property while directing the Treasury Department to hold them in a “custodial and governmental capacity” and to follow the disbursement instructions of Secretary of State Marco Rubio.

The website of Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control’s now instructs parties making payments to Venezuela to deposit the money instead into something called the “Foreign Government Deposit Funds” account. Before receiving payment instructions, a depositor must provide the State Department with information about the parties, the underlying contract, invoices, the amount, the currency, the payment date and the specific license authorizing the transaction. Treasury can apparently reject a deposit if those requirements are not satisfied.

In January, Rubio told the Senate Foreign Relations Committee that approximately $500 million in proceeds had been deposited into a bank account in Qatar that was allegedly owned by Venezuela but controlled by the U.S. He added that $300 million had been transferred to the Venezuelan government to meet public-sector payroll, while another $200 million remained in a short-term account. Rubio also said that Treasury had a written agreement with Venezuela for reviewing its budget requests.

Then, in June, Rubio stated that the Venezuelan revenue was instead being held in a Treasury-blocked Citibank account, with KPMG engaged to audit expenditures. To date, the account number, its balance, the banking agreement, the list of authorized signatories, and a transaction-by-transaction ledger have not been disclosed to Congress or the public.

Alongside Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.), Rep. Sean Casten (D-Ill.) has asked Bessent at two congressional hearings and through multiple letters for the administration’s legal authority for the operation, the written agreement with Venezuela, and rudimentary information about the accounts and the disposition of the money.

When Casten asked at a Sept. 15 House Financial Services hearing which U.S. bank was holding the funds, Bessent demurred. After Casten reminded him that Rubio had already named Citibank, Bessent agreed that Citibank was involved, but would not confirm the amount being held. As to whether the accounts involved only oil proceeds, Bessent stated: “It is many Venezuelan assets.” Astonishingly, he could not confirm that the money was not flowing to U.S. persons.

The executive order’s legal justification for this operation rests largely on the International Emergency Economic Powers Act , which gives presidents authority to regulate, block and control transactions involving foreign property during a declared national emergency. But Article I of the Constitution gives Congress the power of the purse, and nothing in the act or any other federal law authorizes such a colossal power grab.

The executive order doesn’t just freeze Venezuelan property, after all. It also purports to create a comprehensive system for the collection of Venezuelan oil proceeds and other Venezuelan assets, and to give Rubio the power to decide what to do with the “custodial” accounts it creates for holding them.

In short, the government is collecting and controlling another country’s sovereign assets while the Treasury secretary continues to deny Congress an accounting of the location the money, the identity of the account holder, the nature and amount of the payments being made or the identities of the people or entities receiving them. Trump is treating it all as a discretionary executive fund.

Of course, Venezuela’s interim government has a powerful economic incentive to cooperate. It needs access to its oil revenue and other assets to pay government workers and keep functioning. Meanwhile, Trump continues to conduct lethal strikes on Venezuelan fisherman in violation of international law .

The problem here isn’t Venezuela. It is Trump.

Kimberly Wehle is currently a thematic group coordinator and fellow at the Netherlands Institute for Advanced Study in the Humanities and Social Sciences and author of “How to Read the Constitution — and Why,” as well as “What You Need to Know About Voting — and Why” and “How to Think Like a Lawyer — and Why. “

articles.title: Fareham and Gosport volunteers bake free birthday cakes for kids
articles.summary: The Hampshire group says it has seen a rise in demand and it needs more volunteer bakers.
articles.body:
Volunteer bakers are paying out of their own pockets so children in need do not go without a cake on their birthdays.

Free Cakes for Kids Fareham and Gosport buys the ingredients, bakes and delivers cakes for young people whose families are unable to provide one.

Natalie Parker, who joined as a baker while on maternity leave in 2024 and now runs the group, said the thought of a child not having a birthday cake was "heart-breaking".

The group, part of a national network, said demand had risen and it was on the hunt for more volunteers.

Parker said she had seen the group advertised on Facebook and had thought about joining for a while.

"I was on maternity leave with my son and just wanted something to occupy my brain a bit, so I took the plunge," she told BBC Radio Solent.

She said her own son sometimes struggled to understand why other children would go without.

"I can't imagine my own son not having a birthday cake. When I'm baking them, he says to me, 'Why don't they?' He can't, as a child, see why," she said.

The group does not deal directly with families. Referrals come through organisations like food banks, churches and schools.

More stories from Hampshire & the Isle of Wight

Listen to the latest news from Hampshire and the Isle of Wight

Requests are posted in a private Facebook group where volunteers can take them on, often tailoring cakes to a child's favourite characters or interests.

The volunteers buy the ingredients, bake the cakes and deliver them, with the group only able to provide toppers, boards and boxes when it has managed to raise money.

"It's not cheap, especially with food costs going up," Parker said.

"But it's a small price, for me and I know for our volunteers, to pay for that child getting a birthday cake that they otherwise wouldn't be able to have."

The group has more than 30 bakers, ranging from home bakers who make one or two cakes a year to professionals with their own baking businesses.

"You don't need to be an incredible baker to join us," Parker added.

articles.title: Head of Eiffel Tower to resign after controversial order to female staff
articles.summary: Female staff were instructed to remain out of sight during the visit of a Hindu religious group.
articles.body:
( NewsNation ) — The head of the Eiffel Tower is stepping down after female staff were told to stay out of sight during a visit by a Hindu religious group.

Patrick Branco Ruivo, head of the operating company that runs the famous landmark , will leave his job by the end of the year.

The decision follows an internal investigation into a management order requiring female staff to keep hidden during a visit by the Bochasanwasi Akshar Purushottam Swaminarayan Sanstha spiritual movement.

The order caused a staff strike, closing the monument for one day, with tower employees denouncing policies that sidelined female staff in a statement.

The Bochasanwasi Akshar Purushottam Swaminarayan Sanstha movement, known as BAPS, is part of a conservative sect of Hinduism. The group reportedly requested that interactions with women be limited because several monks there took vows forbidding contact with women.

The group later apologized for any inconvenience or offense caused by the request.

Staffers said they found the instructions that ran contrary to French values of equality and nondiscrimination.

articles.title: Execution of US murderer Christa Pike halted shortly before it was due to happen
articles.summary: Pike was convicted and sentenced to death in 1996 for the murder of Colleen Slemmer.
articles.body:
The execution of Tennessee inmate Christa Pike has been halted just over an hour before it was due to happen.

Pike, 50, has been awaiting execution since she was convicted and sentenced to death in 1996 for the murder of Colleen Slemmer.

In their ruling on Wednesday, judges from the Sixth Circuit Appeals court said they needed more time to consider the arguments in Pike's case. It is unclear how long the pause will last.

This latest ruling comes after the Supreme Court denied a reprieve and the Tennessee governor declined to grant Pike's request for clemency earlier this week.

Her lawyers said that for years, the state of Tennessee argued in court that Pike had lied about being sexually abused as a child.

But at a recent hearing about her execution method, the State said it does not dispute she suffered sexual abuse and rape.

Pike's legal team asked the appeals court to send her motion back to the district court, arguing that if the federal courts based their ruling on the state's earlier claim that she was lying, then the federal review was affected.

The appeal that led to Wednesday's stay is different from that made to the Supreme Court, which refused to hear Pike's appeal.

It came from her challenge to Tennessee's lethal injection method, which Pike's lawyers said could cause suffering beyond what is needed to carry out the death sentence - something the Constitution does not allow. The lawyers argued that Tennessee's procedures had denied Pike a fair chance to prove this.

"We will continue to advocate for the lawfully imposed sentence as the courts work through this technical issue," Tennessee's Attorney General said in a statement.

"It is common in capital cases for the defence to raise last minute objections following decades of litigation in numerous courts. We are asking the Supreme Court of the United States to lift the stay."

She was 18 when she and her then-boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, beat, tortured and murdered Colleen Slemmer, a 19-year-old they met at a job training camp for troubled teens.

The murder created a media frenzy in Knoxville, Tennessee in 1995, when the teen was found with a pentagram - a symbol that is associated with satanic groups - carved into her chest. Pike has denied carving the pentagram herself.

She had accused Slemmer of insulting her and trying to steal her boyfriend. Two other residents at the camp later testified that Pike had bragged about the murder before and after and showed them a piece of Slemmer's skull.

A year later, Pike was sentenced to death, while Shipp - who was 17 at the time - was given a life sentence with the possibility of parole.

Pike has a documented history of childhood sexual abuse, abandonment and neglect. Her lawyers believe that if she was found guilty of the same crime today as a teenager she would not receive a death sentence.

Last year, Tennessee's Supreme Court ruled Pike had not shown circumstances that would justify commuting her sentence.

At the time of her incarceration, Pike was the youngest person on death row, according to the Tennessee Department of Corrections.

articles.title: Ethiopia fighting escalates in Tigray killing 52 civilians in Alamata, medic tells the BBC
articles.summary: The deadly fighting has also spread to neighbouring regions, stranding tourists in Lalibela.
articles.body:
At least 52 civilians have been killed during three days of heavy fighting around Alamata in Ethiopia's northern Tigray region, hospital sources have told the BBC.

It appears government troops have taken control of the town from regional fighters and intend to push north towards Mekelle, the region's main city. Social media clips show army tanks on Alamata's streets.

Clashes broke out last week after months of tension between the government and the party that controls Tigray, with both accusing each other of violating a 2022 deal that ended a two-year civil war.

Fighting has also affected neighbouring regions with 33 tourists stranded for the last week in Lalibela, a Unesco world heritage site.

"We have heard fighting, gunfire and artillery cannons firing throughout the week," a British tourist, who asked not to be named, told the BBC's Newsday programme about clashes near Lalibela in the Amhara region.

He said there was a large military presence in Lalibela, famous for being home to 13th Century churches hewn from rock and a holy site for millions of Orthodox Christians.

Most visitors to the tourist hub had been unable to leave since the airport closed to commercial flights last Wednesday, though he said 14 Israeli tourists had been evacuated by military helicopter on Monday.

The fighting around Lalibela has involved the army and an Amhara militia that has allied with Tigrayan fighters.

Earlier in September, they joined forces with other Ethiopian armed movements to form a seven-member alliance with the stated intention of removing the government in the capital, Addis Ababa.

There is also a fear that neighbouring Eritrea could be drawn into the conflict - as the government accuses Asmara of supporting the armed groups, something it denies.

The BBC is unable to report from Tigray and surrounding areas and it is difficult to find out what is happening because communications to the region have been cut.

The two sides disagree over who started the latest fighting.

Are Ethiopians marching back to war in Tigray?

WATCH: Why are Ethiopia's rebels joining forces?

The Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), the party that runs Tigray, says it was responding to a federal offensive, including drone strikes, while the government says Tigrayan forces attacked first after seizing control of airports in the region.

TPLF fighters are also fighting in the Afar region, in a strategic area which connects landlocked Ethiopia to Djibouti and its ports.

Over the last few days, medical charity Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) said more than 700 wounded people had been admitted to hospitals it supports in Tigray.

The doctor at Alamata General Hospital, who requested anonymity, told the BBC the fighting in and around the town had taken place between Saturday and Monday, and involved heavy explosives and artillery, some of which landed in residential homes.

Those killed in the crossfire included children as young as three days old, mothers and cattle herders.

Twelve people had died in a single strike on the town's marketplace, the medic said.

Since the fighting erupted, banking services in Tigray have been suspended by the government. Access to the internet has also been cut - though it is not clear who ordered the closure.

A separate source in Alamata told the BBC there was a worsening humanitarian crisis in the area, as the town swelled with people fleeing fighting.

"All the residents of the surrounding areas entered the town of Alamata by walking on foot for as long as an hour, hoping the town would be safe.

"Unfortunately, everything is blocked - no banking service, no money transfer, no power, no internet, no phone. Hence people are in crisis, simply suffering, everyone is desperate and frustrated."

The British tourist in Lalibela said online banking was working in Lalibela but there was a shortage of physical cash.

He said the situation around the town had calmed down in the last two days and there were indications the airport, which was still being used by the military, might reopen on Thursday.

"The local people, they are still scared of what might happen. The military presence here in the town has remained and a larger military force has been seen leaving the town heading north," he said.

When the airport was first closed, 53 tourists had been in the town, he explained.

But some had since been evacuated, including the 14 Israelis airlifted out on Monday while another five had left the day before via an NGO convoy, despite advice not to travel by road.

Of the remaining tourists in Lalibela, the largest group were Americans, with Israelis, Britons, South Korean, South Africans, an Ethiopian-New Zealander and a Mexican also stranded, he said.

Meanwhile, for those cut off in Tigray because of the telecoms shutdown, the Tigray Broadcasting Service (TBS), based in Addis Ababa, has started an initiative to help reconnect families.

The broadcaster has said it will collect video messages via its Telegram channel from people outside the region and air them via satellite TV.

While limited to greetings and updates, this will provide a rare lifeline for families separated by the blackout.

The clampdown on Tigray's banking services is also affecting Tigrayans who are not physically in the region.

Customers have told the BBC that bank accounts opened in Tigray have been frozen or restricted.

"I boarded public transport from Addis Ababa to Adama and tried to pay using a mobile transfer, but it didn't work," said a former Mekelle resident who moved to the capital two months ago because of growing tensions in Tigray.

"It has created havoc for many people like me who escaped the situation in Tigray," he told the BBC's Tigrinya service.

articles.title: Lindsay Clancy holdout juror’s lawyers say they plan bar complaint against Reddington
articles.summary: Lindsay Clancy's defense lawyer Kevin Reddington faces a bar complaint from attorneys for the holdout juror who blocked her acquittal at trial.
articles.body: PLYMOUTH, Mass. — Two attorneys for the lone holdout juror in the mistrial of Massachusetts woman Lindsay Clancy in the strangling deaths of her three young children say they plan to file a bar complaint against the 36-year-old's defense lawyer over his treatment of their client. "I can tell you, we're gonna file a bar complaint," attorney Tyler Cox told Fox News' Sean Hannity on his namesake show Tuesday evening. Kevin Reddington, a veteran Massachusetts defense lawyer, said in court Tuesday that he was fed up with being accused of "persecuting" the holdout, who was the only man on the 12-person jury who wanted to find Clancy guilty. ATTORNEY FOR LONE HOLDOUT JUROR IN LINDSAY CLANCY MISTRIAL PUSHES BACK ON CLAIMS OF REFUSING THE LAW "He said that all he's done is file a motion," Cox said. "Well, even if you take that as true, which it obviously isn't, the motion that he filed was unprecedented. articles.title: We fear for our lives after being told our abusive exes will be freed from jail early
articles.summary: Three victims of domestic abuse tell the BBC why they feel let down by the early prisoner release scheme.
articles.body:
Three women who have been told their abusive ex-partners will be released early from jail as part of controversial plans to free up prison space have said they fear for their safety.

Around 700 offenders will leave prison in England and Wales on Thursday under the government's early prisoner release plan - with a further 3,800 scheduled for release over the next year.

Ahead of the releases, victims have been sent letters informing them that their attackers will be let out early.

Claire Milne's ex-husband, Robert Dales, was convicted in March this year of coercive control and possessing offensive weapons, including samurai and ninja swords. He was sentenced to three years in prison.

"There was physical violence," said Milne. "There were threats to kill, there was punching of doors, punching of walls. I trod on egg shells throughout the entire relationship and it was almost like I had to coach myself into what to say just to ensure there wouldn't be an escalation."

The Ministry of Justice (MoJ) recently told her Dales, 36, would be released early.

"I am scared that he will come after me. I don't want to die," she said. "I am not a silly woman - I know that I've been in a very high-risk domestic abuse relationship and I know what he's capable of because I lived it."

She said she was "incredibly angry" with the government, who were "not listening to victims".

It comes as prison staff have told the BBC they are increasingly having to put inmates in cells that are unsuitable because of the lack of space. They argue there is no choice but to release more prisoners as room is urgently needed.

Prisons across England and Wales are at 98% capacity, with the latest government figures showing there are just 1,134 spaces remaining in the adult male prison estate. The lowest figure of vacant beds this year.

Under the new scheme, inmates serving sentences of up to 19 months will be released after completing a third of their jail term. Most will have expected to spend 40% of their sentence behind bars - with the remainder served in the community.

The MoJ said that while domestic abuse had a "profound and lasting" impact on victims, the government was committed to keeping the most dangerous prisoners behind bars.

It said offenders jailed for rape, child sex abuse offences and manslaughter would stay in prison, but going further than that would risk the prison system collapsing.

An MoJ spokesperson said the government was investing £1bn in support services, including placing domestic abuse specialists in 999 call centres.

In April, former primary school teacher Christopher Haynes was sentenced to 21 months in prison after admitting to coercive control against his now ex-wife, who has also been notified of his early release.

Karen Haynes told the BBC she was distraught and said it was "a punch in the gut".

"We have fought so hard and we have had to use every inch of the system to get justice," she continued. "I just find it devastating that somebody [who] can admit all of that can be released after only doing seven months of a custodial sentence."

She has been told her ex-husband will now be released in November.

"He always made Christmas so hard," said Karen. "We were constantly scared, we wanted one Christmas without him and without us being frightened he will turn up - but it looks like we won't even get that now."

'Like the rug has been pulled out from underneath me'

Another victim, Alice - not her real name - was subjected to domestic abuse. Her perpetrator is due to be released later this month. She has asked that we do not name her or her ex-partner because she is frightened of what he might do.

"I am terrified," she said. "I had only just started to feel safe and to process what I had gone through."

She said she felt like "the rug had been pulled out from underneath me".

From 13 October, governors will release a second tranche of 650 prisoners who have been serving sentences of between 19 months and two years and five months. Inmates will be released in nine tranches until June next year.

Those serving longer sentences - including more dangerous criminals - will not become eligible for the scheme until next year. They had previously expected to spend two thirds of their sentence behind bars, but instead will complete half of their term in prison before spending the rest of their punishment in the community on licence.

Dame Nicole Jacobs, the domestic abuse commissioner for England and Wales, called the scheme "shameful" and said she's had "no assurance that the danger perpetrators pose has been properly considered and assessed with meaningful input from victims".

"Ultimately, we cannot ignore the fact that the early release scheme has caused untold damage to victims' confidence in the justice system," Dame Nicole added.

She said Prime Minister Andy Burnham "must take urgent steps to address this" and called on the probation service to be given "the resources it needs to safely manage more offenders in the community". She also called for additional funding for domestic abuse services to support victims.

A recent report raised serious concerns about electronic tagging, which can be used to monitor offenders' movements in the community. It found almost half of tags were not fitted on time.

Alice told the BBC she had been looking to buy a doorbell with a camera fitted to help make her feel safer, but said she cannot afford one. "I don't feel prepared in the slightest and I don't feel safe," she added.

"I think the early release scheme is a joke to victims and survivors, who spent years preparing for trial, going through evidence and re-traumatising themselves to go to court, just for the perpetrator of their crimes to be released after just 33% of their sentence".

The MoJ said: "Anyone who is released faces the toughest-ever controls on their movements, including world-first restriction zones and the largest expansion of electronic tagging, with victims having a say in their perpetrators' licence conditions."
