articles.title: Britain believes Iran was involved in incident near air base used by U.S., Prime Minister Andy Burnham says
articles.summary: There are strong indications that Iran played a part in an incident outside a U.K. airbase that U.S. forces use to strike Iran, Prime Minister Andy Burnham said.
articles.body: LONDON — There are strong indications Tehran played a part in a security incident outside a British air base that U.S. forces use to facilitate strikes on Iran, Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Wednesday. Burnham said he had chaired an emergency security meeting this week after the incident, which unfolded in the early hours of Sunday. Five men, all British nationals, were arrested on suspicion of terror and explosives offenses and were released on bail earlier this week. “We have been waiting to confirm what we could say, but we can now confirm our belief that Iran played a part,” he said in an interview with Sky News. ”This remains, though, a complex and very serious police investigation, so I can’t say any more at this stage,” he added. The British Parliament is in recess, but Burnham said he “wouldn’t hesitate” to recall lawmakers “should that be necessary.” Iran has denied any involvement in the incident. “The embassy of the Islamic Republic of Iran in London categorically rejects and strongly condemns the recent unfounded and malicious speculations published by some British individuals and media outlets attempting to link Iran to arrest of five suspects in the vicinity of RAF Fairford base,” the Iranian Embassy in Britain said in a statement on X on Monday. Burnham’s statements were based on intelligence that has been gathered as a result of the investigation into the incident, two senior intelligence officials briefed on the matter told NBC News. There were two calls that were made early Sunday morning U.K. time that alerted authorities that the five individuals could have been up to something inappropriate, according to one official. One call to police came from one of the five men in the group at approximately 12:45 am local time, the official said. British media previously reported this call. A second call was placed by a local farmer to police around 1:30am local time — a call that was cited by police initially as the reason for the tip on the group’s activities, according to the official. So far, no charges have been filed against the men, all in their 20s and from London, who were arrested after three vehicles were seen moving toward RAF Fairford, a British air force station about 90 minutes west of London. Counterterrorism police later took over the case after a major incident was declared and dozens of homes were evacuated, disrupting life in the normally quiet, rural community of the Cotswolds. Residents were allowed to return home Monday. In an update Tuesday, the head of counterterrorism policing, Laurence Taylor, said no explosives had been found in three vans belonging to the suspects, although “a quantity of petrol” had been recovered. “Those vehicles have been subject to extensive examination, with the support of military assets and forensic experts, and we can confirm that no improvised explosive devices were found,” he said, adding that investigators had searched properties in London. In the United Kingdom, police can usually hold people for up to 24 hours before they have to charge or release them, although officers can apply to extend that time if they suspect a serious crime has been committed. Suspects arrested under the Terrorism Act can be held without charge for up to 14 days. Tuesday’s update came after President Donald Trump told reporters he was disappointed about the decision to free the men on bail. “I’m just disappointed that they caught terrorists — they did a good job, and then they sort of let them go,” he said, adding, “How do you give bail to a terrorist?” Asked if it was a long-standing investigation, Trump replied, “A long-standing. Yeah, we were involved in it.” “They put them out on bail. I assume they have, they have them watched closely. But these were serious people, seriously bad people, and they should not have done that,” he added. Burnham said Wednesday that the men were released with the “strictest possible bail conditions,” telling the BBC: “The authorities have this under the strongest grip and closest control, and I can assure you of that.” Separately, Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the incident “clearly involves the hands of a foreign actor” — an allegation British officials had not confirmed until Burnham’s comments Wednesday. Burnham’s predecessor, Keir Starmer, gave permission for the United States to use its bases for “specific and limited defensive” operations against Iran. Earlier this year, the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps told the semiofficial Tasnim news agency that “any base used to facilitate aggression against Iranian territory is considered a legitimate target,” specifically citing bomber flights taking off from Fairford.

articles.title: Syria removed from US arms export ban list
articles.summary: US has gradually loosened restrictions placed on Syria during the Assad era to aid country’s recovery from conflict.
articles.body:
The United States has removed Syria from a list of countries banned from buying or importing US weapons as Washington continues to strengthen ties with the government in Damascus.

The US Department of State said on Wednesday that it was changing the International Traffic in Arms Regulations, or ITAR, to remove Syria from the list and allow US arms sales on a case-by-case basis.

“On August 19, 2026, the Secretary of State approved a new defence trade policy for Syria that would permit the review of defence article and defence service transfers to Syria on a case-by-case licensing basis,” the note, posted on the Federal Register Wednesday, reads.

“The Secretary directed the Department to codify this change by publishing an amendment to the ITAR removing Syria from the list of countries for which it is the policy of the United States to deny licenses and other approvals for exports and imports of defence articles and defence services destined for or originating in those countries.”

The change is the latest instance of the Trump administration easing previous restrictions placed on Syria during the decades-long rule of the al-Assad family, which ended with the ouster of former President Bashar al-Assad by rebels in December 2024.

The country’s current president, Ahmed al-Sharaa , has placed a strong focus on improving relations with the US and obtaining relief from economic sanctions that he says hinder the country’s path to recovery after years of devastating civil war. Al-Sharra is a former fighter who was aligned with Syria’s al-Nusra Front armed group.

The Trump administration, expressing optimism about its relationship with the new Syrian government, has gradually loosened a number of restrictions.

Trump eased some economic sanctions last year, and US Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced in August that the US was removing Syria’s designation as a “state sponsor of terrorism”.

The US also announced in February that it planned to eventually reopen its embassy in Damascus, which has been closed since 2012.

articles.title: UK believes Iran ‘played a part’ in foiled attack, Burnham says
articles.summary: British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Wednesday his government believes that Iran “played a part” in the alleged thwarted attack on a U.S. air base in the United Kingdom earlier this week. “There are strong indications that Iran played a part in what happened over the weekend at RAF Fairford,” Burnham told the BBC, referring…
articles.body:
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Wednesday his government believes that Iran “played a part” in the alleged thwarted attack on a U.S. air base in the United Kingdom earlier this week.

“There are strong indications that Iran played a part in what happened over the weekend at RAF Fairford,” Burnham told the BBC , referring to the air base about 90 miles west of London in the county of Gloucestershire.

“We will say more in due course, but we can confirm our belief that we believe Iran to have played a part,” he added.

He did not give further details as to what evidence his government had found to support such a conclusion, though Tehran has strongly denied any involvement in the incident.

British authorities on Sunday arrested five men on explosives and terror charges near RAF Fairford after a local farmer called police over three suspicious vehicles and men wearing masks near the base late Saturday night.

Police later said the vehicles did not contain any explosives and the men, all five of whom are British nationals in their 20s, were released on bail a day later on Monday.

It was also found that one of the men had dialed the police himself, nearly an hour before the farmer called authorities.

President Trump has criticized the British government for its decision to release the men on bail, telling reporters Monday he was “surprised that they released them,” adding, “I wouldn’t have done that.”

Trump also has contradicted British officials in insisting the U.S. government worked with the U.K . in arresting the suspects, telling reporters Sunday the men were “under view for a long time.”

Questioned about why police had released the suspects on bail, Burnham told the BBC that the men were subject to strict conditions.

“I think people need to understand that when it says released, that isn’t as people might think. It’s obviously with the strictest possible bail conditions,” he said. “The authorities have this under the strongest grip and closest control, and I can assure you of that.”

The prime minister added that his government has been “talking to our counterparts in the United States all week to explain what is happening here, how things are being done,” and he said he has “complete confidence in the way British security services are handling this.”

“Of course it remains an ongoing, complex and serious police investigation, and of course we are working closely with our colleagues in the United States of America,” he added.

Burnham’s comments follow those from Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who said Monday that the incident at RAF Fairford “clearly involves the hands of a foreign actor.”

American B-52 and B-1 bombers have taken off from RAF Fairford as part of the U.S. military campaign against Iran . The air base in southern England is owned by the U.K. and operated by American forces.

Tehran in July threatened that “any base used for aggression against Iranian territory constitutes a legitimate target for our forces” raising fears across Europe of a terrorist attack during the now seven-month conflict.

But the Iranian Embassy in the U.K. said in a Monday statement that it “categorically rejects and strongly condemns the recent unfounded and malicious speculations” regarding the Islamic Republic’s potential role in the incident.

articles.title: Russia warns NATO of possible nuclear response if Kaliningrad is cut off
articles.summary: Moscow claims that NATO is preparing an air and naval blockade in the Baltic Sea.
articles.body:
Russia has warned NATO it is prepared to use its entire arsenal, including nuclear weapons, if the Western alliance attempts to cut off the Baltic exclave of Kaliningrad , according to a diplomatic document sent to member states.

The diplomatic memo sent on Wednesday claimed Moscow has “information that NATO is preparing an air and naval blockade of Kaliningrad”.

NATO’s response came through its Secretary-General Mark Rutte, who said that NATO is a defensive alliance and that Russia should “stop the nuclear threats”, calling the document unhelpful.

Rutte also downplayed the seriousness of the threat, saying that “Putin knows that he can never win” in a direct escalation with NATO.

Bordered by Poland and Lithuania, both NATO members, the Russian territory of Kaliningrad sits on the Baltic Sea . The region serves as a major military outpost, housing Russia’s Baltic fleet and nuclear-ready Iskander missile systems.

The exchange comes more than four and a half years into Russia’s full-scale war in Ukraine, as tensions increasingly spill into neighbouring states.

Poland has heightened its air defence posture following alleged incursions into its airspace in recent weeks, while Danish authorities said a Russian warship fired two flares near a Danish military helicopter over the Baltic Sea two weeks ago.

articles.title: An Iowa developer bought the 58-acre Valley West Mall for $11 million; a nearly 50-year-old JCPenney lease now stands in the way of redevelopment as the city considers up to $110 million in incentives
articles.summary: An Iowa developer has bought the 58-acre Valley West Mall site for $11 million (£8.2 million).
articles.body: An Iowa developer has bought the 58-acre Valley West Mall site for $11 million (£8.2 million). The company is now starting a major redevelopment project, but it must first deal with complex lease agreements and get support from the city. Brian Martin, president and chief executive officer of Threshold Capital and Threshold Development, completed the purchase of the long-troubled West Des Moines shopping center. His company plans to turn the large site into a mixed-use area with retail, housing, and entertainment. The project is expected to cost between $300 million and $350 million. However, the master plan depends on solving several legal and financial issues. The biggest challenge is a long-standing lease with department store giant JCPenney. The developer must also get city approval for public financing incentives.Anchor tenant holds long-term lease rightsA key part of the redevelopment is a nearly 50-year-old lease held by JCPenney, one of the property's original anchor tenants. According to reporting by the Business Record, the current agreement gives JCPenney major control over operations and the power to block major changes around its part of the property. The lease limits where new buildings, multi-family housing, or internal roads can be built without the company's approval. Developer Brian Martin said dealing with the anchor store's lease is an important step in completing the overall site plan. "It's going to be transformational," Martin told the Business Record about his plans for the property. "It's going to be a very vibrant development. It will be very well thought out." Talks between Threshold Capital and retail leaders are still taking place. At the same time, architects are working on a site plan that respects JCPenney's rights while allowing the rest of the property to be developed.Municipal incentives under considerationTo help pay for the large project, local government leaders in West Des Moines are considering major public financing options. As reported by television station KCCI, city officials have considered providing up to $110 million in public funding incentives. The proposed package would use tax increment financing, public infrastructure spending, and possible site improvements to help cover the early costs of removing the enclosed mall. The city council previously made the Valley West area an urban renewal district. This created a legal system for using future property tax revenue from the new development to help pay for public works, parking facilities, and utility improvements at the site. City planners say public investment is needed to address the area's commercial decline. The area has seen lower foot traffic and retail store closures over the past decade.Vision for a modern commercial hubValley West Mall opened in 1975 and was a major shopping center for central Iowa for four decades. Changes in shopping habits and competition from outdoor lifestyle shopping centers led to years of store departures, financial problems, and eventually foreclosure proceedings before the recent sale. Under Threshold Capital's plan, the enclosed shopping center would be replaced by an open-air village-style development. It would include high-density housing, office space, restaurants, and public civic plazas. "It's going to be something unique to the area that West Des Moines can be proud of," Martin told the Business Record. He said early plans include major architectural water features and public lighting installations. Martin said early interest from possible retail, commercial, and residential tenants has been strong. However, formal leases will not be signed until city approvals and site plans are completed.Next steps for site clearanceBefore demolition can begin, Threshold Capital must submit a final site plan to the West Des Moines Plan and Zoning Commission and City Council. The developer expects to present final architectural plans after lease talks with JCPenney are resolved. If the city approves the incentives and the site plans pass regulatory review, the first stages of construction and infrastructure work on the 58-acre property could begin later. articles.body: Mhow: An unidentified person allegedly smashed a window of a roadside-parked car and stole cash and valuables near Tanda town in Dhar district late Tuesday evening.ASI Ram Singh Hathila said the incident occurred near the river bridge on Rajgarh-Kukshi road, about two kilometres from Tanda. Tanda police registered a theft case under Section 303(2) of BNS following a complaint by the car owner.Cash worth Rs 1.56 lakh and gold ornaments were stolen from the car parked near a river in Sanawadiya village, complainant Satyendra (44), a resident of Param Vihar Colony, told police.
